reason: Grouping fibres seems like the first step toward building a muscle that can pull on the arm.
expectation: I expect a bundle of muscle fibres, though it may still need a sheath and attachment to bone.

alternatives.reason: Adding blood vessels may support the arm, but building the muscle seems more directly tied to the goal.

effect: The fibres form a bundle, so adding the sheaths looks like the next step toward an organized muscle.
reaction: The paired poses help connect the individual shortening fibre to the bundle.
reason: Connective tissue sheaths should organize and support the bundle as part of a muscle.
expectation: I expect a sheathed muscle bundle or a more complete muscle, though it may still need attachment to the arm.

alternatives.reason: Blood vessels may support the arm, but I want to continue building the muscle first.

effect: The sheaths formed a biceps with tendons, showing how fibre pulls reach bone and why an opposing muscle is needed.
reaction: The explanation of tendons carrying the pull makes the construction clearer.
reason: Adding blood vessels to the skeleton is the only offered combination and should help build the arm.
expectation: I expect an arm skeleton supplied with blood vessels; I am unsure how it will connect to the muscles next.

effect: The arm assembly has flexor and extensor slots, so the biceps and triceps can now be fitted on opposite sides.
reaction: The explanation makes their opposing roles clear, although the blood vessels' role in creating the assembly is less clear.
reason: Fit the biceps into the flexor position to begin adding the opposing muscles.
expectation: I expect the biceps to fill the flexor slot, leaving the extensor slot for the triceps.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also belongs on the assembly, but either muscle appears suitable to fit first.

effect: The biceps is fitted, leaving the triceps to complete the opposing pair.
reason: The triceps is the only offered combination and should fill the extensor position.
expectation: I expect the triceps to be fitted opposite the biceps, completing the opposing muscles.

effect: The triceps is fitted alongside the biceps; the arm assembly still needs shoulder and hand tissues.
reason: Adding the remaining tissues is the only offered combination and should complete the arm.
expectation: I expect a more complete arm with the opposing muscles in place, though I am unsure whether that will complete the goal.

effect: Adding the shoulder and hand tissues completed the supplied moving arm and the chapter goal.
reaction: The completed arm brings the parts together, though the final picture description adds little explanation of how they work together.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making the biceps was the strongest moment: the explanation connected the fibres, connective tissue and tendons to a pull on bone, and explained why an opposing muscle is needed.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the two muscles was predictable and repetitive, with little feedback beyond confirmation that each part was fitted.

surprise.text: The sheaths gathering into tendons clarified how the pull from muscle fibres reaches bone.

arbitrary.text: Adding blood vessels to the skeleton produced an arm assembly with muscle slots, but the result did not explain why that combination created the assembly.

continue.text: I would be somewhat interested in another chapter because the connection from fibres to tendons and opposing movement was clear, although I would hope for more meaningful choices and explanations than the later fittings offered.
